stories.headline: Half-brother of musician Billy Strings sentenced to 48 years for 2020 murder of Denver guitarist
stories.summary:
Patrick Apostol, 48, was sentenced Monday to 48 years in prison for the second-degree murder of 31-year-old Zackary Smith, a Denver guitarist found shot in the head inside a rolled-over car in an alley near Quince Street and East 17th Avenue in the East Colfax neighborhood in 2020. A Denver jury convicted Apostol in June after investigators tied him to the killing through gunshot residue found on a black robe he wore the day of the murder and deleted text messages.

The case went unsolved for three years until Lakewood police received a community tip in 2023 and arrested Apostol, who had lived in the area and was interviewed by officers on the day of the crash. Investigators determined Smith had been in a relationship with Apostol's then-girlfriend, establishing a motive.

Apostol is the half-brother of Grammy Award-winning bluegrass performer Billy Strings, whose legal name is William Lee Apostol. Strings publicly stated he had little relationship with the man, having met him only around age 12. Denver District Attorney John Walsh called Smith's murder 'a terrible tragedy for everyone who knew him and loved him both in Denver and beyond.'

stories.headline: Denver pet daycare owner cited for animal cruelty after dog dies in hot car outside facility
stories.summary:
The owner of Happy Tail Happy Dog, a pet daycare and boarding facility at 4352 Cherokee St. in Denver, has been cited for animal cruelty after a dog died of apparent heat exposure in a vehicle parked outside the business on Aug. 26, city officials announced Tuesday. The incident was not reported to Denver Animal Protection until Sept. 11, roughly two weeks after the dog's death.

The Denver Department of Public Health and Environment said a criminal case is expected to be filed in Denver District Court later this week. The facility lists two owners, Ted Gualtier and Julian Hogan, but officials did not specify which individual was cited.

'This is a sad reminder that animals should never be left alone in the car for any period of time,' said department spokesperson Ryann Money, noting that interior car temperatures can rise nearly 20 degrees within the first 10 minutes. Residents who observe a pet locked in a hot car can call Denver Animal Protection at 720-913-2080.

stories.headline: Denver mayor, clerk sue Trump administration to block ICE agents from polling locations
stories.summary:
Denver Mayor Mike Johnston and City Clerk and Recorder Paul Lopez have joined civil rights groups in filing a lawsuit against the Trump administration to prevent Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents from being stationed near polling locations during the November election. The city announced the legal action on Monday.

The lawsuit reflects ongoing tensions between Denver city government and federal immigration authorities ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. City officials argue that the presence of ICE agents at or near polling places would intimidate voters and suppress turnout, particularly among immigrant communities.

Denver has been a flashpoint in disputes between local government and federal immigration enforcement throughout the Trump administration's second term. The city's action follows a series of confrontations over local cooperation with federal immigration policy.

stories.headline: Aurora City Council moves to restrict data centers and new turf to conserve water amid severe drought
stories.summary:
The Aurora City Council unanimously gave initial approval Monday to two water conservation ordinances in response to severe drought conditions affecting Colorado. The first measure would ban evaporative cooling systems within the city, with data centers — which consume large volumes of water to cool servers — as a primary target.

The second ordinance would prohibit installation of cool-season grasses such as Kentucky bluegrass without prior written approval from the city manager, while still allowing warm-season turf varieties that use 60 to 70 percent less water. The measure also bans new ornamental water features without approval and restricts spray irrigation in non-high-traffic areas from October through April.

Aurora Water's General Manager Marshall Brown noted that irrigation systems were activating as early as February this past winter. Both measures will require final approval votes at the next council meeting in two weeks. Aurora is also planning additional rules for data centers, including restrictions on where they can locate and how close they can be to homes and schools.

stories.headline: Colorado River basin officials authorize continued emergency releases from Flaming Gorge to protect Lake Powell
stories.summary:
Upper Colorado River Basin officials agreed Monday to extend emergency water releases from Flaming Gorge Reservoir in Wyoming through April in an effort to stabilize dangerously low levels at Lake Powell. Since April, the Bureau of Reclamation has already released about 450,000 acre-feet from Flaming Gorge toward Powell, and an additional 550,000 acre-feet are planned, bringing the total to 1 million acre-feet.

Lake Powell currently holds about 22 percent of its total capacity following a record-poor winter that sharply reduced snowmelt flows into the Colorado River system. The basin's overall storage has fallen to about one-third of capacity. Blue Mesa Reservoir, the largest in Colorado, held just 20 percent of capacity as of Sept. 8, leaving Flaming Gorge as the only reservoir with sufficient water for emergency releases.

Officials warned that if Powell drops below a critical elevation of 3,510 feet, Glen Canyon Dam's ability to generate hydropower and eventually release water at all could be compromised, threatening water supplies for millions of people in Arizona, California, Nevada and Mexico. Recovery of Flaming Gorge will depend on future Rocky Mountain snowpack.

stories.headline: Colorado Democrats target rural voters with expanded county-level investment ahead of November midterms
stories.summary:
The Colorado Democratic Party is doubling down on investments in rural and conservative counties ahead of the November midterm elections, building on a 2024 strategy that party leaders say produced measurable gains in traditionally red areas. State party chair Shad Murib said tens of thousands of dollars were invested in rural and red counties during the last cycle.

The party is operating a grant program that provides funding to local county parties for grassroots organizing and support for local candidates running in competitive or conservative districts. Las Animas County is among those receiving support this cycle.

The effort reflects a broader Democratic strategy to reverse rural vote losses that have cost the party competitive ground across Colorado and nationally. Whether the increased investment will translate into significant vote shifts in deeply conservative areas remains to be seen ahead of the Nov. 3 election.

stories.headline: Mormon church's real estate arm moves to develop 960-acre Tributary community near Denver airport
stories.summary:
Property Reserve Inc., the real estate investment arm of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, is developing Tributary, a 960-acre master-planned residential community south of Denver International Airport and east of E-470 in Aurora. The church began quietly acquiring agricultural land in the area during the 1970s and 1980s, decades before DIA opened in 1995, and farmed the parcels through leases as suburban growth slowly encroached.

Once complete over the next two to three decades, Tributary is expected to add more than 12,000 residents to Aurora's population. Plans call for two commercial and retail areas, multiple parks, trails, a recreation center, a school and a fire station. The project sits within the 21,000-acre Denver Aerotropolis development zone, which spans parts of Denver, Aurora and Adams County.

The move marks a significant shift for Property Reserve, which historically focused on passive land accumulation in agriculture and ranchland before pivoting to active master development in the 2000s. The church's real estate arm has developed major residential communities in Utah, Florida and Arizona, with its Sunbridge project in Florida — covering 27,000 acres with 36,000 planned homes — serving as its flagship. Bloomberg estimates the church owns at least 2.4 million acres nationally with an assessed value exceeding $20 billion.

stories.headline: I-70 to close over Kipling Street in Wheat Ridge for two consecutive weekends for bridge repairs
stories.summary:
The Colorado Department of Transportation announced multiday closures of Interstate 70 over the Kipling Street bridge in Wheat Ridge during the next two weekends for bridge repair work. The first closure will affect westbound I-70 beginning at 7 p.m. Friday and lasting through 6 a.m. Tuesday; the second will affect eastbound I-70 from 7 p.m. Sept. 25 through 6 a.m. Sept. 29.

During the closures, motorists will not be able to enter or exit I-70 at Kipling, and Kipling itself will be closed in both directions at the interchange to allow detoured traffic to use on- and off-ramps. Each closure is expected to last up to 83 hours, with CDOT warning of delays of 30 minutes or more.

Westbound travelers can use West 44th Avenue to Ward Road as a detour, while eastbound drivers should use West 44th Avenue to Wadsworth Boulevard. Bicyclists and pedestrians will be rerouted via Garrison Street. Drivers can sign up for project alerts by texting I70REPAIRS to 21000 or checking COtrip.org.

stories.headline: Lincoln Hills, Colorado's historic Black mountain resort, gains new attention amid DEI rollbacks
stories.summary:
Founded in 1922 by two Black entrepreneurs from Denver's Five Points neighborhood, Lincoln Hills was the first mountain resort west of the Mississippi created by and for Black Americans, offering a safe retreat in Gilpin County's Coal Creek Canyon when racial hostility — including a resurgent Ku Klux Klan in 1920s Denver — barred Black Coloradans from most other leisure destinations. The 650-acre retreat attracted luminaries including Duke Ellington, Langston Hughes and Zora Neale Hurston before closing in 1965.

Advocates and descendants are now working to preserve and promote Lincoln Hills as the federal government rolls back diversity, equity and inclusion programs nationally. History Colorado recently revamped its museum exhibit on Lincoln Hills, adding new stories and memorabilia, while the nonprofit Lincoln Hills Cares manages most of the remaining 100 acres and is seeking expanded revenue to protect the site, which was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1980.

Denver entrepreneur Morgan Ramsey, 33, is developing a luxury travel experience rooted in Black history at Lincoln Hills through her company TELA, pitching the site as 'the Martha's Vineyard of the West.' Retired Denver judge Gary Jackson, whose great-grandfather was among the first cabin builders there, said the site represents 'the ingenuity and courage of Black people' and deserves wider recognition among Coloradans.

stories.headline: Mountain lion tranquilized, relocated after taking up residence in Westminster tree near Standley Lake
stories.summary:
Colorado Parks and Wildlife officers tranquilized and relocated a mountain lion Tuesday morning after the animal was spotted in a tree on Eaton Street between 112th and 113th avenues in Westminster, prompting police to close the block for roughly 90 minutes. The lion had been observed in the area and near Standley Lake over the previous several days and was not moving out of the suburbs on its own, according to CPW spokesperson Kara Van Hoose.

The relocation is the second of a metro-area mountain lion this year. A separate lion was removed from near Cherry Hills Village in Arapahoe County in May. Tuesday's animal was found just inside the Jefferson County boundary with Adams County; CPW said no lion had been relocated from Adams County since at least 2019.

An estimated 3,800 to 4,400 mountain lions live in Colorado, with most inhabiting foothills, canyon and mesa terrain. Wildlife officials noted that late summer and early fall typically bring increased lion sightings in suburban areas as the animals follow deer moving to lower elevations.

stories.headline: Cole Carrigg homers twice as Rockies end eight-game losing streak with 9-3 win over Padres
stories.summary:
Rookie outfielder Cole Carrigg homered twice and went 4 for 5, finishing a triple shy of the cycle, as the Colorado Rockies defeated the San Diego Padres 9-3 at Coors Field on Tuesday night to snap an eight-game losing streak. Carrigg's three-run shot to right field capped a five-run sixth inning that gave Colorado a four-run cushion in the first multi-homer game of the 24-year-old's career.

Ryan Feltner earned the win after allowing five hits with five strikeouts across five scoreless innings in relief of starter Kyle Freeland. Troy Johnston added three hits and two RBIs, and TJ Rumfield extended his on-base streak to 20 games.

The victory was a rare bright spot for a Rockies team that entered 5-21 in its previous 26 games and stands at 56-95 overall. Colorado must win at least seven of its final 11 games to avoid becoming the first franchise with four consecutive 100-loss seasons since the 1962-65 New York Mets. The loss snapped an eight-game winning streak for the Padres, who remained 2.5 games ahead of Arizona for the final National League wild card.

stories.headline: Semitrailer rollover on I-76 in northeast Colorado kills 10 cattle, closes highway for six hours
stories.summary:
A semitrailer hauling cattle rolled over on Interstate 76 in northeast Colorado early Tuesday, killing 10 animals and closing the highway for more than six hours before it reopened by 9:30 a.m. The crash occurred at about 2:58 a.m. when the westbound truck entered the median and overturned near Hillrose, roughly 11 miles east of Brush, spilling its cargo across the roadway.

Three other semitrailers and one car subsequently struck cattle that had been scattered in the crash. Of the 48 head of cattle originally in the truck, 10 were found dead, 29 survived, and nine remained missing as of Tuesday morning. The driver of the cattle hauler was transported to a hospital, though the extent of injuries was not immediately available.

The Colorado State Patrol managed closures on westbound I-76 between Merino and Colorado 63 and eastbound I-76 between U.S. 6 and Hillrose in addition to the primary closure near the crash site. All closures had been lifted by mid-morning. The cause of the crash remained under investigation.

topStory.headline: Kennedy Center Board Votes to Close Building as Judge Blocks Trump Name Addition
topStory.summary:
The board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted Tuesday to close the Washington landmark, marking the third such vote since February and coming within an hour of a federal judge blocking the board from adding President Donald Trump's name to the building. Trump, writing on Truth Social, said the closure would take effect "immediately" and announced he would withhold a planned $257 million renovation unless courts ruled in favor of placing his name on the institution. He also said the Department of Justice would seek an expedited appeal and vowed to take the matter to the Supreme Court if a lower court ruling went against him.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper issued the written order blocking the name addition shortly before the board vote, ruling that a board resolution approving the inscription "Renovated and Restored by President Donald J. Trump" violated both his earlier order and a statute enacted by Congress. "Simply put, defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress's blessing," Cooper wrote. Despite the board's vote, the center cannot close without Cooper lifting a separate temporary block he imposed in May requiring the institution to remain open while litigation proceeds; a request to lift that block is expected by Friday.

The dispute stretches back to early 2025, when Trump replaced several board trustees in February and the reconstituted board moved to rename the institution. New lettering bearing Trump's full name was affixed to the center's front portico, and the board subsequently approved a resolution in August to rename the campus "President Donald J. Trump Plaza" if $100 million in private funds was raised. Those changes prompted cancellations by artists and a reported drop in ticket sales, with Congress having separately approved more than $250 million for long-planned renovations.

Ohio Democratic Congresswoman Joyce Beatty, an ex officio board member who brought the legal challenge, accused Trump of a "breach of his fiduciary duty as a trustee" and said his attempted renaming had driven audiences and artists away from the center. Beatty told MSNBC that Trump had called into the board meeting and, upon learning she had prevailed in court, engaged in "name calling" in what she described as "the most unprofessional thing" she had ever witnessed. Her attorneys, Norm Eisen and Nathaniel Zelinsky, said in a joint statement that the shutdown vote was an attempt to "hide the terrible mismanagement under its current leadership."

The outcome of the pending court proceedings will determine whether the center closes and whether the planned renovations move forward. Trump said he has raised $17 million in private funds to help keep the center financially solvent in the interim. The Kennedy Center was established by Congress as a living memorial to President John F. Kennedy, and any permanent renaming or structural changes to that designation would require congressional approval, according to the judge's ruling.
